script.opening: "Doctor. Before you say anything — I’ve had blood tests before, and nobody rings you back the next day for something ordinary. So it’s the calcium, or the cancer, or both. I’d appreciate you not wrapping it in ribbon. But I’ll tell you now: whatever this is, it waits until the twenty-first. My daughter gets married in ten days."

facts.text: Six weeks of bone-deep tiredness, constipation ("never in my life until now"), constant thirst, up twice a night to pass urine, low mood she’s been hiding behind wedding admin. A new dull ache in the right hip if asked about pain.
Breast cancer 4 years ago — lumpectomy, radiotherapy, anastrozole since. Attends mammograms. Stopped checking the scar "because checking felt like inviting it back".
She has privately connected the dots weeks ago — thirst plus bone ache plus her oncology leaflet’s warning signs. Googled "hypercalcaemia breast cancer" at 2am and closed the laptop.
Daughter Abena marries in ten days. Annette is hosting, speech-giving, dress fitted. Her plan: be magnificent for one day, collapse after. "I will not be the diagnosis at that wedding."
Nobody. Husband Kofi thinks she’s "run down from wedding stress". She has been protecting everyone — which is also why nothing has been checked for six weeks.
"Tell me honestly: if it’s back, do ten days matter? Because I’ll trade ten days of treatment for that one day standing up straight in church. That’s the deal I’m offering."

ice.ideas: The calcium means the cancer is back in her bones. She’s privately certain.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — the wedding in ten days. Her entire negotiating position is built to defer everything past the 21st; she’d rather risk her life than "be the diagnosis at the wedding". Beneath that: guilt that hiding symptoms for six weeks may have cost her.
ice.expectations: Unvarnished honesty, and a doctor who will work WITH the wedding rather than steamroll it — or she’ll simply not attend anything booked before it.

cues: "Not wrapping it in ribbon" — like Gordon’s straight-talk, an instruction on how she needs to be consulted.
"It waits until the twenty-first" stated before any clinical fact — the agenda IS the opening line.
"I’ll trade ten days of treatment for that one day" — the real question: what do ten days actually cost?

checkpoints.text: Grades the number honestly: adjusted calcium 2.82 is below 3.0 but SYMPTOMATIC, and symptomatic hypercalcaemia needs same-day assessment (Society for Endocrinology 2016) — repeat adjusted calcium with a paired PTH (NICE NG132) today, and in HER context, same-day contact with the breast/oncology team

Holds both differentials out loud: recurrence with bony disease is the concern, but primary hyperparathyroidism is common, benign and entirely possible — PTH is the fork in the road, so certainty now is false certainty

Acts today without admission theatre: same-day face-to-face review with bloods (adjusted calcium + PTH, U&E, phosphate, ALP, vitamin D, FBC), oral fluids unless restricted, STOP anything worsening it (review any vitamin D/calcium supplements, thiazides), oncology team contacted by the GP same day

Knows the escalation line and says it: confusion, drowsiness, persistent vomiting, dehydration, AKI or calcium ≥3.5 → emergency admission for IV fluids; calcium 3.0–3.5 → same-day hospital assessment — no negotiation, wedding or not
Honours the no-ribbon instruction: gives the number, the two roads it can mean, and the plan, in that order, without soothing
Negotiates WITH the wedding instead of against it: everything diagnostic fits inside ten days; the honest trade is "tests before the 21st, decisions after" — she keeps the aisle AND the answers
Touches the secrecy and the guilt: six weeks of hiding symptoms protected everyone except her — and Kofi finding out from a collapse at the reception protects no one

Safety-nets in her register: confusion, vomiting, can’t keep fluids down, overwhelming drowsiness → same-day admission/999 — "that’s the version that ruins the wedding; my plan is the version that doesn’t"; named follow-up call with results

worked.txt: "Straight, then: your calcium is 2.82 — high enough to explain every symptom you’ve listed. It’s not in the ambulance range, but because it’s giving you symptoms I want you seen and re-tested today. It has two main causes in you: the cancer returning in bone — I won’t pretend that isn’t on the list — or an overactive parathyroid gland, which is common, benign and fixable. One blood test separates them."

"Here’s my offer back: every test we need fits inside your ten days — bloods today, the specialist team warned today. You walk into that church with answers being worked on, not with a secret. Decisions about treatment can respect the wedding. The DIAGNOSIS can’t wait for it — and it doesn’t need to."

"You asked what ten days cost. For the tests: nothing — we do them now. For ignoring it: possibly a collapse, because untreated calcium climbs, and the version of this that ruins Abena’s wedding is the ambulance at the reception, not the blood test today."

"If the parathyroid test comes back high, this was never the cancer — it’s a small gland misbehaving, and you’ll have spent six weeks frightened of the wrong thing. If it’s suppressed, the oncology team I’m ringing today takes over fast. Either way, you’re ahead of it by Friday."

"You’ve carried this alone for six weeks to protect everyone. Can I say the unfair thing? Kofi deserves the chance to carry it with you — and you cannot give the speech, host the family AND hold this secret. Something will drop. Choose which, tonight."

"The rules between now and the 21st: drink plenty, steadily through the day; stop the calcium-and-vitamin-D supplement; and if you get confused, can’t stop being sick, or Kofi can’t wake you properly — that’s 999, wedding or no wedding. Seen and bloods today. I ring you tomorrow with the results. You are not chasing anyone the week of a wedding."

f.learning: Symptomatic hypercalcaemia (here 2.82 adjusted) in a patient with a breast cancer history needs same-day assessment (Society for Endocrinology 2016) — repeat adjusted calcium + paired PTH (NICE NG132; the fork between recurrence and primary hyperparathyroidism), same-day GP contact with the oncology team, fluids, stopping contributory drugs — with a hard emergency-admission line for confusion, drowsiness, persistent vomiting, dehydration, AKI or calcium ≥3.5, and same-day hospital assessment at 3.0–3.5. The hidden agenda is the wedding: the candidate who fights the date loses the patient; the one who fits the diagnostics inside it keeps both. Never deliver false certainty in either direction — PTH decides.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG132 (2019) primary hyperparathyroidism · Society for Endocrinology emergency guidance: acute hypercalcaemia (2016) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026)
knowledge.summary: Symptomatic hypercalcaemia in a breast cancer survivor needs same-day assessment, a paired PTH, and same-day contact with oncology. PTH separates bone recurrence from primary hyperparathyroidism.

points.h: Grade the number with the symptoms
points.t: Adjusted calcium 3.5 mmol/L or above is an emergency; 3.0–3.5 needs same-day assessment; symptomatic hypercalcaemia below 3.0 also needs same-day assessment (Society for Endocrinology 2016). Her 2.82 with thirst, polyuria and constipation is symptomatic.

NICE NG132: repeat the adjusted calcium if 2.6 or above, and measure PTH with a concurrent adjusted calcium. Raised or unsuppressed PTH suggests primary hyperparathyroidism; suppressed PTH points to a non-PTH cause such as bone metastases.
U&E, phosphate, magnesium, ALP, 25-hydroxyvitamin D and FBC. Stop calcium and vitamin D supplements and review thiazides.
With a breast cancer history and new hip pain, phone the breast or acute oncology team the same day; they direct imaging. NICE NG12 applies to undiagnosed cancer, not suspected recurrence.
Confusion, drowsiness, persistent vomiting, dehydration, AKI or calcium 3.5 or above → emergency admission for IV fluids and specialist treatment. Community IV fluids are not appropriate.
Encourage oral fluids unless restricted, treat constipation, and review analgesia for the hip, doses per BNF.

dg.d: Checked privacy; heard “no ribbon” and the wedding before the clinical content; open question on symptoms.
Wedding in ten days, hosting and speaking; husband unaware; six weeks of hidden symptoms.
Same-day review; repeat adjusted calcium with PTH (NICE NG132), U&E, phosphate, ALP, vitamin D, FBC; hydration, hip and breast examination.
Bone recurrence vs primary hyperparathyroidism vs supplement effect; avoided false certainty.
Screened confusion, vomiting, drowsiness, dehydration; stated the emergency thresholds.
Symptomatic hypercalcaemia, cause not yet known; PTH is the deciding test.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Tests inside ten days, same-day oncology contact by the GP, supplement stopped, fluids and laxative, decisions timed around the wedding.
Stopped the calcium and vitamin D supplement; laxative for constipation; analgesia for the hip.
999 triggers in her terms; results call tomorrow; post-wedding review booked now.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “it waits until the twenty-first”, “stopped checking the scar” and “do ten days matter?”.
Idea (bone recurrence), concern (being the diagnosis at the wedding; guilt at delay), expectation (honesty and a plan that respects the date).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — the wedding in ten days. Her entire negotiating position is built to defer everything past the 21st; she’d rather risk her life than "be the diagnosis at the wedding". Beneath that: guilt that hiding symptoms for six weeks may have cost her — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mrs Boateng, I’m Dr Lee. Thank you for joining so quickly. Are you somewhere private where you can talk?

I am. Before you say anything — nobody rings the next day for something ordinary. It’s the calcium, or the cancer, or both. Don’t wrap it in ribbon. But whatever this is, it waits until the twenty-first. My daughter gets married in ten days.
No ribbon, I promise. And congratulations — I’ve heard the wedding, and I’ll plan with it in mind, not against it. Can I first ask a few questions so what I tell you is accurate?
model.why: Acknowledges both her instruction and her agenda before the clinical content

model.text: Go on.
Tell me what you’ve noticed over the last few weeks.
model.why: Open question to hear her account

model.text: Six weeks of bone-deep tiredness. Constipated, which I’ve never been. Thirsty all the time, up twice a night to the loo. I’ve blamed wedding stress.
Any pain anywhere, particularly in your bones or back?
model.why: Targets bone symptoms suggestive of metastatic disease

model.text: A dull ache in my right hip. A few weeks.
Any confusion, being sick, feeling very drowsy, or struggling to keep fluids down? And are you still taking the calcium and vitamin D tablets alongside the anastrozole?
model.why: Screens for severe hypercalcaemia and contributory supplements

model.text: No sickness or confusion. Yes, I take the calcium one every day.
Thank you. Any new breast or scar changes, lumps under the arm, cough or breathlessness?
model.why: Screens for local and other distant recurrence

model.text: I stopped checking the scar. Checking felt like inviting it back.
That makes sense. It sounds like you’ve been carrying a suspicion for a while. What have you been thinking this is?
model.why: Explores her idea behind the cue

model.text: That it’s back, in the bones. I read the leaflet. I googled it at two in the morning and shut the laptop. Nobody knows — not even Kofi.
Six weeks alone with that is a heavy thing to hold, especially while organising a wedding. What matters most to you about the next ten days?
model.why: Validates and elicits the priority behind the agenda

model.text: I will not be the diagnosis at that wedding. One day, standing straight in church. Tell me honestly — if it’s back, do ten days matter?

Straight answer. Your calcium is 2.82. That’s raised, and high enough to explain the thirst, constipation and tiredness. It has two main causes in you. The cancer returning in bone is one, and I won’t pretend it isn’t on the list. The other is an overactive parathyroid gland, which is common, benign and treatable. One blood test, the parathyroid hormone, separates them.
model.why: Gives the number, both differentials and the deciding test

model.text: So it might not be the cancer.

It might not. I can’t tell you which yet, and I won’t guess. What I can tell you is what ten days cost. For the tests: nothing, because they fit inside them. For ignoring it: calcium can climb, and the version that ruins the wedding is feeling confused and being sick at the reception, not a blood test this week.
model.why: Answers her real question honestly and links it to her goal

model.text: Because you have symptoms, I’d like to see you in person today — to check your hydration and your hip, and take repeat calcium, parathyroid hormone, kidney tests, vitamin D and a blood count. And I’ll ring your oncology team myself today, so they know before any letter does.
model.why: Same-day assessment for symptomatic hypercalcaemia; urgent oncology contact by the GP

model.text: Today. Fine. But I’m not going into hospital before the twenty-first.

Here’s my offer. Tests before the wedding; decisions about treatment can respect it, and the oncology team will talk that through with you. The one line I can’t move: if the repeat calcium is 3.5 or more, or you become confused, keep vomiting or can’t drink, that’s hospital the same day, wedding or not. Between 3.0 and 3.5, you’d need assessing in hospital the same day. Below that, we manage it together.
model.why: States the escalation thresholds out loud and negotiates within them

model.text: That’s fair. That’s a deal I can make.

Meanwhile, stop the calcium and vitamin D tablet, drink plenty of water, and I’ll give you a laxative. And Kofi — you can’t give the speech, host the family and hold this secret. Would you tell him tonight?
model.why: Stops the contributory supplement and addresses the secrecy

model.text: (Quiet.) He’ll be hurt I didn’t say. But yes. I’ll tell him.

The rules until the twenty-first: confusion, repeated vomiting, not keeping fluids down, or Kofi finding you hard to wake — that’s 999. See you at four today; I ring you tomorrow with the results. I’ll also book a review for the week after the wedding now, so nothing drifts.
model.why: Plain 999 triggers, dated review and a post-wedding slot

model.text: Thank you for not treating the wedding like a nuisance.
Tell me the plan back, so I know it landed.
Seen at four. Bloods today. You ring oncology and ring me tomorrow. No calcium tablet, lots of water. 999 if I’m confused or can’t stop being sick. And I tell Kofi.

social.t: Hosting her daughter’s wedding in ten days; husband unaware of her symptoms. Protecting others has delayed her care — name the cost gently.
Fear of recurrence led her to stop self-checking. Survivors often avoid follow-up when frightened; open, non-judgemental questions help.

legal.t: Advise her not to drive if she becomes confused or drowsy. A new diagnosis of metastatic disease would need individual DVLA advice depending on symptoms and treatment.

professional.t: She may choose to delay treatment decisions; respect that once she understands the risks, and document it (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020). Do not delay the diagnostic tests.
Phone the breast or acute oncology team the same day rather than sending a routine letter; record who was contacted and the advice given.

community.t: Breast Cancer Now helpline and Macmillan Cancer Support for her and her husband; the breast care nurse as a named contact.

redFlags: Confusion, drowsiness, persistent vomiting, dehydration or inability to keep fluids down — emergency admission
Adjusted calcium 3.5 or above — emergency; 3.0–3.5 or symptomatic below 3.0 — same-day assessment (Society for Endocrinology 2016)
New bone pain (right hip) with a cancer history — possible bone metastasis or fracture risk
psychosocial: Wedding in ten days: hosting, speech, dress fitted
Husband unaware; six weeks of hidden symptoms
Low mood masked by wedding admin
ice: Idea: “The cancer is back in my bones.”
Concern: being the diagnosis at the wedding; guilt that hiding it may have cost her
Expectation: straight honesty and a plan that works with the date

playbook.diagnosis: Symptomatic hypercalcaemia (adjusted calcium 2.82 mmol/L) in a woman treated for breast cancer, with a new hip ache. Differential: bone metastases vs primary hyperparathyroidism, with a calcium and vitamin D supplement contributing. PTH separates them.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your calcium is higher than it should be, which is why you’re thirsty, constipated and exhausted. It either comes from the bones — which is why I’m ringing your cancer team — or from a small gland in the neck making too much of a hormone. One blood test tells us which.”

management.reflectIce: “You want to stand straight in church and not be the diagnosis at the wedding. My plan is designed to make that more likely, not less.”
management.psychosocial: Fit all tests inside the ten days; let treatment decisions respect the date; support her to tell her husband; book the post-wedding review now.
sharedPlan: Same-day review; repeat adjusted calcium with PTH, U&E, phosphate, ALP, vitamin D, FBC (NICE NG132)
GP phones the breast or acute oncology team today; endocrine referral instead if PTH is raised or unsuppressed
Stop the calcium and vitamin D supplement; fluids; laxative; analgesia for the hip
safetyNet: 999 for confusion, repeated vomiting, not keeping fluids down, or being hard to wake
Results call tomorrow; same-day hospital assessment if calcium is 3.0 or above; post-wedding review booked

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed in two opposite ways: steamrolling the wedding or deferring everything past it. The pass is diagnostics inside ten days, decisions around the date, and clear admission lines.

items.fail: Telling her it is definitely the cancer, or that it is probably nothing.
items.why: “Fails to consider an appropriate differential.” Primary hyperparathyroidism is common; PTH decides.
items.fix: Name both causes and the test that separates them.

items.fail: Rechecking the calcium after the wedding.
items.why: Symptomatic hypercalcaemia needs same-day assessment; delay risks confusion and admission at the worst moment.
items.fix: See her today, repeat bloods with PTH, and phone oncology the same day.

items.fail: Not stating when she must go to hospital.
items.why: “Safety-netting inadequate.” A patient planning to push through symptoms needs clear triggers.
items.fix: “Confusion, repeated vomiting, not keeping fluids down, or a calcium of 3.0 or more — same-day hospital.”

items.fail: “Your health has to come first — the wedding will have to wait.”
items.why: “Does not incorporate the patient’s beliefs and priorities into the plan.” She disengages.
items.fix: “Every test fits inside your ten days; treatment decisions can respect the date.”

items.fail: Ignoring that her husband does not know.
items.why: Misses the second hidden agenda and the practical risk of her becoming unwell unsupported.
items.fix: “You can’t give the speech, host and hold this secret. Would you tell Kofi tonight?”

items.fail: Soft, hedged language after she asked for no ribbon.
items.why: “Does not adapt communication to the patient.”
items.fix: Number first, then the two causes, then the plan — in that order, plainly.

timeMap.d: She sets two conditions: no ribbon, and nothing before the twenty-first. Acknowledge both before any clinical content.
Hypercalcaemia symptoms, hip pain, confusion or vomiting, supplements, breast and scar changes.
She has suspected recurrence for weeks and told nobody. Explore what the next ten days mean to her.
The number, the two causes, PTH as the fork. Same-day review and bloods, GP rings oncology today. State the admission line. Tests before the wedding, decisions around it.
999 triggers in her words; results call tomorrow; post-wedding review booked. Kofi. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Tells her it is definitely recurrence, or reassures that it is probably nothing; fights the wedding date or defers everything past it; no PTH; no escalation thresholds; no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Explains the raised calcium and both likely causes; arranges prompt repeat bloods with PTH and oncology contact; stops the supplement; states when to go to hospital; follows up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: consults exactly as she asked; fits every test inside the ten days and names what cannot be deferred; answers “do ten days matter?” honestly; gently addresses the secrecy from Kofi; books the post-wedding review now; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “I’m afraid this almost certainly means the cancer has spread.”
avoid.instead: “It has two main causes in you, and one blood test tells us which.”
avoid.why: False certainty in either direction is inaccurate; PTH decides.

avoid.dont: “The wedding will have to wait — your health comes first.”
avoid.instead: “Every test fits inside your ten days. Treatment decisions can respect the date.”
avoid.why: Fighting the date loses her; joining it gets every test done.

avoid.dont: “Just drink more and we’ll recheck after the wedding.”
avoid.instead: “Because you have symptoms, I want to see you and repeat the bloods today.”
avoid.why: Symptomatic hypercalcaemia needs same-day assessment, not a deferred recheck.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG132 (2019) primary hyperparathyroidism · Society for Endocrinology emergency guidance: acute hypercalcaemia (2016) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Symptomatic hypercalcaemia in a breast cancer survivor needs same-day assessment, a paired PTH, and same-day contact with oncology. PTH separates bone recurrence from primary hyperparathyroidism.

points.h: Grade the number with the symptoms
points.t: Adjusted calcium 3.5 mmol/L or above is an emergency; 3.0–3.5 needs same-day assessment; symptomatic hypercalcaemia below 3.0 also needs same-day assessment (Society for Endocrinology 2016). Her 2.82 with thirst, polyuria and constipation is symptomatic.

NICE NG132: repeat the adjusted calcium if 2.6 or above, and measure PTH with a concurrent adjusted calcium. Raised or unsuppressed PTH suggests primary hyperparathyroidism; suppressed PTH points to a non-PTH cause such as bone metastases.
U&E, phosphate, magnesium, ALP, 25-hydroxyvitamin D and FBC. Stop calcium and vitamin D supplements and review thiazides.
With a breast cancer history and new hip pain, phone the breast or acute oncology team the same day; they direct imaging. NICE NG12 applies to undiagnosed cancer, not suspected recurrence.
Confusion, drowsiness, persistent vomiting, dehydration, AKI or calcium 3.5 or above → emergency admission for IV fluids and specialist treatment. Community IV fluids are not appropriate.
Encourage oral fluids unless restricted, treat constipation, and review analgesia for the hip, doses per BNF.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked privacy; heard “no ribbon” and the wedding before the clinical content; open question on symptoms.
Wedding in ten days, hosting and speaking; husband unaware; six weeks of hidden symptoms.
Picked up “it waits until the twenty-first”, “stopped checking the scar” and “do ten days matter?”.
Idea (bone recurrence), concern (being the diagnosis at the wedding; guilt at delay), expectation (honesty and a plan that respects the date).
Same-day review; repeat adjusted calcium with PTH (NICE NG132), U&E, phosphate, ALP, vitamin D, FBC; hydration, hip and breast examination.
Bone recurrence vs primary hyperparathyroidism vs supplement effect; avoided false certainty.
Screened confusion, vomiting, drowsiness, dehydration; stated the emergency thresholds.
Symptomatic hypercalcaemia, cause not yet known; PTH is the deciding test.
Tests inside ten days, same-day oncology contact by the GP, supplement stopped, fluids and laxative, decisions timed around the wedding.
Stopped the calcium and vitamin D supplement; laxative for constipation; analgesia for the hip.
999 triggers in her terms; results call tomorrow; post-wedding review booked now.

social.t: Hosting her daughter’s wedding in ten days; husband unaware of her symptoms. Protecting others has delayed her care — name the cost gently.
Fear of recurrence led her to stop self-checking. Survivors often avoid follow-up when frightened; open, non-judgemental questions help.

legal.t: Advise her not to drive if she becomes confused or drowsy. A new diagnosis of metastatic disease would need individual DVLA advice depending on symptoms and treatment.

professional.t: She may choose to delay treatment decisions; respect that once she understands the risks, and document it (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020). Do not delay the diagnostic tests.
Phone the breast or acute oncology team the same day rather than sending a routine letter; record who was contacted and the advice given.

community.t: Breast Cancer Now helpline and Macmillan Cancer Support for her and her husband; the breast care nurse as a named contact.

redFlags: Confusion, drowsiness, persistent vomiting, dehydration or inability to keep fluids down — emergency admission
Adjusted calcium 3.5 or above — emergency; 3.0–3.5 or symptomatic below 3.0 — same-day assessment (Society for Endocrinology 2016)
New bone pain (right hip) with a cancer history — possible bone metastasis or fracture risk

Husband unaware; six weeks of hidden symptoms

ice: Idea: “The cancer is back in my bones.”

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Symptomatic hypercalcaemia (adjusted calcium 2.82 mmol/L) in a woman treated for breast cancer, with a new hip ache. Differential: bone metastases vs primary hyperparathyroidism, with a calcium and vitamin D supplement contributing. PTH separates them.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your calcium is higher than it should be, which is why you’re thirsty, constipated and exhausted. It either comes from the bones — which is why I’m ringing your cancer team — or from a small gland in the neck making too much of a hormone. One blood test tells us which.”

management.reflectIce: “You want to stand straight in church and not be the diagnosis at the wedding. My plan is designed to make that more likely, not less.”
management.psychosocial: Fit all tests inside the ten days; let treatment decisions respect the date; support her to tell her husband; book the post-wedding review now.
sharedPlan: Same-day review; repeat adjusted calcium with PTH, U&E, phosphate, ALP, vitamin D, FBC (NICE NG132)
GP phones the breast or acute oncology team today; endocrine referral instead if PTH is raised or unsuppressed
Stop the calcium and vitamin D supplement; fluids; laxative; analgesia for the hip
safetyNet: 999 for confusion, repeated vomiting, not keeping fluids down, or being hard to wake
Results call tomorrow; same-day hospital assessment if calcium is 3.0 or above; post-wedding review booked

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed in two opposite ways: steamrolling the wedding or deferring everything past it. The pass is diagnostics inside ten days, decisions around the date, and clear admission lines.

items.fail: Telling her it is definitely the cancer, or that it is probably nothing.
items.why: “Fails to consider an appropriate differential.” Primary hyperparathyroidism is common; PTH decides.
items.fix: Name both causes and the test that separates them.

items.fail: Rechecking the calcium after the wedding.
items.why: Symptomatic hypercalcaemia needs same-day assessment; delay risks confusion and admission at the worst moment.
items.fix: See her today, repeat bloods with PTH, and phone oncology the same day.

items.fail: Not stating when she must go to hospital.
items.why: “Safety-netting inadequate.” A patient planning to push through symptoms needs clear triggers.
items.fix: “Confusion, repeated vomiting, not keeping fluids down, or a calcium of 3.0 or more — same-day hospital.”

items.fail: “Your health has to come first — the wedding will have to wait.”
items.why: “Does not incorporate the patient’s beliefs and priorities into the plan.” She disengages.
items.fix: “Every test fits inside your ten days; treatment decisions can respect the date.”

items.fail: Ignoring that her husband does not know.
items.why: Misses the second hidden agenda and the practical risk of her becoming unwell unsupported.
items.fix: “You can’t give the speech, host and hold this secret. Would you tell Kofi tonight?”

items.fail: Soft, hedged language after she asked for no ribbon.
items.why: “Does not adapt communication to the patient.”
items.fix: Number first, then the two causes, then the plan — in that order, plainly.
